passage: I'm Deepika, and I've shared a flat with Vasudha for three years. She was a translator. Last year her work almost dried up; clients said software could do a first draft. Now she reviews contracts for a law firm, and she's busy.

passage: Ramesh, sit, I'll tell you something. When I was your age, twenty-four, I set type by hand in a printing press. Then computers came. My boss said, 'Learn or leave.' I was angry for a month. I thought, I'm skilled, why should a machine decide? My friend Alka had already joined night classes in computer typesetting. She dragged me along. I was the slowest in class, sitting between college boys. It was embarrassing. But I learned, and within two years I was teaching others at the press. Now you tell me your office is using these AI tools. Don't waste a month being angry like I did. Find out what the new thing can't do, and learn to do that well.

That small project got her first paid UX job. She still takes translation work. Just less of it.

"They're cutting half the translation team," Nitin said, dropping into the chair. "The new AI tool does first drafts now. We just check."
Charu turned down the dal. "Are you in the half?"
"Not this time. Next time, who knows."
"So what do you want to do?"
"Panic, mostly."
She sat down across from him. "After the panic."
He rubbed his face. "The people they're keeping are the ones who fix the tool's mistakes in legal and medical documents. The specialised stuff."
"Could you do that?"
"I'd need to learn legal terms properly. There's a six-month evening certificate at the university."
"Six months of evenings." Charu raised an eyebrow. "You'll be tired and grumpy."
"Very grumpy."
"Then I'm taking over Sunday cooking and you're taking Tuesday dishes. Deal?"
Nitin laughed for the first time that day. "Deal. I'll enrol tomorrow."

I took a free online course at night and redid three old projects as case studies with interviews and findings, not just pretty screens. Being a beginner again at twenty-five was humbling. In March I got my first research contract. I still draw, and I use the AI tools for quick drafts, but my time goes to the part that needs a person.

12 March

The agency sent the new rates today. Translation work is now "post-editing", fixing what the machine writes, at a third of the old pay. Half my regular clients have gone quiet.

I sat by the window for an hour feeling like a typewriter in a museum.

Called Anirban, who ran the Marathi desk before I did. He said, "Dhruv, the machine can't tell if a pharmacy leaflet sounds scary to a grandmother. You can." He's moved into localisation testing, checking whether apps actually make sense to real users in each language.

So, a plan. Not a panic.
1. The six-week evening course in localisation testing Anirban mentioned. Enrol this week.
2. Keep two days for the post-editing work so rent is covered while I learn.
3. Build three sample reports on local apps and show them to Anirban by May.

Still scared. But at least I'm scared with a list.

qa.a: Translation work is now called "post-editing", fixing what the machine writes.

qa.a: Dhruv felt outdated and frightened, "like a typewriter in a museum", after the new rates and clients going quiet.

qa.a: It has a short course, keeps some paid work going while learning, and includes sample reports to show a mentor by a set date.

For fifteen years, the typists sat under the neem tree outside the tehsil office in Samrala, and for the last three, Baljeet had sat among them with his grey machine. Now the land forms were online, and most mornings he typed nothing at all.

His niece Gurleen, home from college, found him oiling the machine for the second time that week. "Chachu, you know the forms better than anyone," she said. "People still don't know how to fill them online."

That night she showed him the government's free course for village computer centre operators. He struggled with the mouse. He felt foolish at twenty-six, learning from a girl of nineteen.

By Baisakhi, he had his certificate. He rented a corner of the photocopy shop, with a second-hand computer and a sign in Punjabi. The first customer was an old farmer from his own village, who said, "Good. Now someone will explain it properly."

Ines had worked as a translator in Lisbon since she was twenty-two. By twenty-five, half her regular clients had switched to machine translation and only sent her "light checks" at a fraction of the fee.
She felt her whole training shrinking. For a month she was bitter and applied for anything.
Her friend Daniel, a software tester, asked what she was actually good at. "Noticing when something sounds wrong to a real person," she said. "Tone. Culture. Jokes that don't land."
"That's a job," he said. "UX writing. Localisation testing."
She took an evening course for three months and built a small portfolio: rewriting app screens so they sounded natural in Portuguese, and finding cultural errors in translated menus. She volunteered for a local nonprofit to get real examples.
In spring, a travel company hired her to check their app's Portuguese version. Machine first, Ines second. She didn't love it all. But she wasn't shrinking anymore.

qa.a: Machine translation.

qa.a: Ines felt bitter and shrinking, as if her whole training was losing value.

qa.q: Which steps made Ines's pivot deliberate rather than random?
qa.a: Identifying her real strength, taking a focused course, building a portfolio and getting real examples through volunteering.

At the bank's regional training centre in Lucknow, Nazia sat in the back row, arms folded. Her teller job was being cut; machines and the app were doing most of it. She was twenty-six and felt old.
The trainer, Minakshi, started with a question: "What did customers ask you that no machine could answer?"
Nazia thought. The elderly man who didn't understand his pension. The woman who was scared of loan papers. "I explained things," she said.
"That's what the customer advisory role needs," Minakshi said. "You'll learn the products and the systems. You already have the patience."
The course was eight weeks: product modules, role-plays, a test. Nazia struggled with the software and stayed back twice to practise. She passed on the second attempt.
Her first week as an advisor, an old man shook her hand for ten minutes after she explained his account. She didn't fold her arms once.

qa.a: Eight weeks.

qa.q: How was Nazia feeling in the back row at the start?
qa.a: Nazia felt defensive and discouraged, arms folded, worried she was too old to change.

qa.q: What helped Nazia retrain successfully?
qa.a: Seeing that her skill of explaining things carried over, then working through the modules and practising the software until she passed.

qa.a: He probably felt relieved and grateful, which is why he shook her hand for ten minutes.

Akash,
You asked why I left the call centre. Honestly, I saw the writing on the wall. Our team went from forty to twelve in a year. The chatbot now answers most questions, and we only get the angry ones.
I'm twenty-five. I didn't want to wait to be let go. So I looked at what's growing where we live: rooftop solar. Every other building in our area is putting panels up, and the installers are always busy.
I did a government-certified course for solar technicians, three months, evenings and weekends. My hands were clumsy at first. I felt stupid next to eighteen-year-olds who'd done wiring since school. But I kept going, and now I'm apprenticed to an installer.
The pay is lower for now. Some days I miss the air conditioning. But I'm learning something no chatbot can do on a roof.
If you want, I'll send you the course details.
Kamal
